title.title: Disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis
title.subtitle: Claim: 3-SAT on $n$ variables is solved, even counted, in $2^{n/(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$ time

plain: Trying all on/off settings of $n$ switches takes $2^n$ steps; ETH said you can't do much better. Claimed: you can

beats.text: ETH: 3-SAT needs time $2^{cn}$ for some fixed $c > 0$
The claimed exponent per variable shrinks like $1/\sqrt{\log n}$, schematically
Shrinking means it drops below every fixed $c$

steps: Write the formula as sparse polynomial equations
Replace them with low-degree forms that share linear summaries
Count the common zeros, which counts the solutions

achievement.label: Impagliazzo–Paturi (2001)
achievement.context: Claim: counting solutions takes $2^{n/(\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}$ time and polynomial space
achievement.note: Still hopeless in practice: the exponent shrinks only by about $\sqrt{\log n}$

verify.detail: Lean: a slightly weaker bound, still subexponential, so ETH still falls
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean scope; the expert working group has not reported

voice.text: Does three SAT really need exponential time?
The hypothesis: two to a fixed fraction of n. The claimed exponent keeps shrinking.
Turn clauses into polynomials, then count their common zeros.

sources.quote: The Exponential Time Hypothesis (Impagliazzo–Paturi 2001) says 3-SAT on n variables needs 2^{Ω(n)} time
Subexponential only by a factor (log n)^{1/2} in the exponent
which refutes ETH; the paper's sharper bound is not in Lean.
